rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The play at a glance "Trifles" by Susan Glaspell (1916) is a one-act murder investigation in which the detectives fail and the wives succeed — and the failure is the point. John Wright has been strangled in his farmhouse bed; his wife Minnie Foster Wright is the suspect. The men — the County Attorney, the Sheriff and the neighbour Mr.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Women find the evidence men dismiss as 'trifles' — gender irony is the core.
The dead canary = motive; discuss the moral choice the women make.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: Gender theme: the men's condescension ('women worry over trifles') is exactly why they fail — quote one condescending line and pair it with the women's discovery.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **Mrs. Hale** is the play's conscience: she knew Minnie Foster as the girl who sang, married a man like "a raw wind" into twenty years of silence, and feels the guilt of the neighbour who never visited. rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Justice versus law** — the central theme: the women find the truth the law cannot see, and the play asks whether concealing evidence can be the more just act. **The oppression of women** — Minnie's life is the case study: childless, voiceless, isolated on a lonely farm, married to a man who silenced her song; the trifles are the archaeology of that oppression.…  ·  ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. Why do the men fail to find the motive? (2 marks)** A. Because they search for evidence in the men's world — the bedroom, the barn, the outdoors — and dismiss the kitchen as unimportant. The motive lies in the domestic details they call trifles, and their contempt for that world is precisely what blinds them. **Q. What is the significance of the dead canary? (2 marks)** A.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Why is the play titled 'Trifles'? (2 marks) — the 'trivial' domestic details the men ignore contain the motive the women uncover.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "The kitchen holds the truth the men cannot find." Discuss how the setting and the trifles solve the case. (8 marks)** A model answer treats the kitchen as the play's real crime scene and walks the evidence in order: the broken preserves (the fire's neglect, the household's stopped rhythm), the quilt's crazy stitching (the mind's record), the broken birdcage hinge (violence in the…  ·  **‘Trifles’ — evidence the women read, men missed (classified)** | Clue | What it shows | Who notices | |---|---|---| | Erratic stitching | Minnie’s mind snapping | Mrs Hale/Mrs Peters | | Dead canary | Killed song = killed spirit | Women | | Empty birdcage | Violence around the bird | Women | | Messy kitchen | Unfinished work = interrupted life | Women | | Cold kitchen fire | Nerve broken mid-task…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The action, scene by scene The play opens in the Wrights' bleak, disordered kitchen the day after the murder. Mr. Hale narrates his visit of the previous day: John Wright dead with a rope around his neck, Minnie rocking and answering oddly — she said she did not wake because her husband slept soundly, and that she did not know who did it.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Symbolism** — the play's master device: the canary is Minnie Foster herself, the girl who sang in the choir before John Wright's silence caged her; the broken cage is the marriage; the wrung neck is what the marriage did; the unfinished quilt is her mind mid-collapse; the cold kitchen and exploded preserves are the household's stopped life.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The title's irony: men dismiss 'trifles' (kitchen things) that actually solve the crime — the women find the evidence the men overlook; this reversal is the core answer.  ·  Trick 2: Evidence of motive: the broken birdcage and the dead canary — Minnie's strangled bird mirrors her strangled spirit; connect symbol to motive.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. What does the dead canary symbolise? (2 marks) — Minnie Foster's silenced joy; her husband killed it as he killed her spirit.
